title: Resolve support tickets faster with full customer context
description: How Strawberry rebuilds a ticket's story across billing, product data, docs, and team chat, then drafts the reply or hands engineering a case it can act on.

navigation.title: Customer Support & Success
navigation.tagline: Resolve tickets faster with every source in view

introduction: A customer sends in a ticket: "I bought credits, they never arrived, and now I can't use the product."
So the chase begins. Open the payment processor. Check the credit ledger, then the account's live balance, then the app logs. Hope the timestamps agree with each other.
Work that makes you feel like a robot should be done by a robot.

Strawberry is a browser with AI companions built in. A companion is an AI teammate that works in the tabs and apps your team is already signed into, so it can run that chase for you: open the records, put the events in order, and keep every claim next to where it came from. The ticket reaches you with the story assembled and a recommendation: answer it, escalate it, or hand it to engineering.
That's how we run our own support. Our companion is called Fritz, and every case on this page came out of its queue, anonymized.

blocks.text: Bring Strawberry the customer work already in front of you: the ticket you have been avoiding, the account that looks quiet, the customer who signed yesterday. Your companion picks the smallest useful piece of it and shows you the result before anything is sent or changed.

skill.context: Here's the ticket I've been avoiding. Tell me what happened before I reply.

sections.title: See the full story behind a ticket

blocks.text: A ticket says what the customer wrote today. The answer usually lives somewhere else: last month's thread, a promise in the CRM, a usage change, a Slack message about a known bug. Strawberry pulls those together before you reply and keeps each claim next to where it came from.
Take the credits that never arrived. Fritz, the companion that handles our own support, checked the payment processor, the credit grant, the usage ledger, the live balance, and the app's event log.

Payment: succeeded. Credits: landed about two seconds later. Complaint: roughly six minutes after that, with no usage in between. The money was right and the balance was right. The customer's window was showing a stale counter.

So no refund and no second grant. The customer needed relaunch steps. Engineering needed to know that a counter can go stale after a top-up. A look at the ticket alone would have produced a kind, fast, wrong answer.

The same habit matters for accounts. One of our customer champions looked inactive: chat usage flat, credit usage flat, the usual cue for a worried check-in. Fritz widened the check to browser and integration activity first and found more than 1,500 background actions across five connected tools in three supposedly quiet days. The champion had stopped typing and let the product run. The second seat on the account had almost nothing, and that was the person who needed onboarding.

items.title: Check whether a quiet account is really quiet
items.text: Usage across chat, browser, and integrations, plus the goals and promises on record, so one flat metric does not send the wrong email to the wrong person.

skill.context: Review the customer's progress, current signals, evidence gaps, and next actions.

items.title: Walk into the renewal knowing what was promised
items.text: Twenty minutes before a check-in, QBR, or renewal call, you need the few things that could derail it: unmet commitments and who made them, usage that dropped, the open ticket nobody mentioned.

skill.context: Prepare for a customer conversation using the account context that could change it.

items.title: Leave the call with a name next to every next step
items.text: Notes that split into customer follow-up on one side and internal actions with an owner on the other.

skill.context: Preserve the decisions, commitments, and follow-through from a customer conversation.

sections.title: Draft the reply from the records

blocks.text: Drop in a ticket or point Strawberry at the queue. It checks the full thread, the customer's history, current docs, known issues, and your team's actual policy before it suggests a reply. Priority and escalation follow your rules, not a severity score it invented.

When Fritz, our support companion, drafted the reply for the missing-credits customer, it did not apologize for a problem that hadn't happened. It confirmed the payment and the grant, with times, explained that the balance on screen was stale, gave the relaunch steps, and said what engineering was looking at.

The opposite mistake is just as easy. A customer wrote in, annoyed that they were paying but being treated as a free user. The account they wrote from was free and had hit its limit. A shallow check would have told them they were wrong.
Fritz compared their other logins, found the paid subscription on a different one, and emailed them which login held the plan. Twelve minutes, complaint to answer.

items.title: Triage the queue by what is at stake
items.text: Priority, next action, and a first response for each ticket, using your team's rules. Forty overnight tickets become the three to read before standup.

skill.context: Triage this customer request using the team's actual rules and current context.

items.title: Investigate before you answer
items.text: The full thread, the account's history, current docs, known issues, and what your team's policy says, reconciled into a reply you can send.

skill.context: Find the strongest available answer and prepare a response for this customer and channel.

blocks.text: Engineering should never receive a link to a mystery ticket. Once you approve the route and the boundaries, Strawberry recognizes when a case needs another team and prepares the handoff: impact, timeline, what has been tried, and the one decision the receiving team owns. Customer-identifying detail stays in support.
One customer told us the app had stopped opening after an update. Seven tries over several days. On its own, that is a low-priority issue called "app won't launch" that waits in a backlog for a week.
Here is what Fritz, our support companion, did with it in under thirty minutes:

items: Joined the support report to release timing, product telemetry, error monitoring, and the relevant source code.
Isolated the failure to a point before the app's first window is even created.
Widened the search to everyone on the same version.
Found dozens of previously active users on that version matching a strict likely-regression definition.
Handed engineering a root-cause analysis and a minimal patch proposal.

blocks.text: One "it won't open" became an incident packet with a cohort attached. Engineering did not have to decide whether to care.

items.title: Send a human the full case
items.text: Impact, timeline, what has been tried, the customer's current message, and the specific decision the receiving team now owns.

skill.context: Prepare the customer-impact brief, current communication, exact internal ask, and next owner.

items.title: Create Jira or Linear issues from support tickets
items.text: Reproduce the problem, check for duplicates, and file an engineering issue that does not leak private customer context.

skill.context: Research and report the product bug while keeping customer-specific context appropriately scoped.

items.title: Keep it visible until it is resolved
items.text: The next update owed, the decision still open, and confirmation that the fix landed, tracked across support and the specialist team.

skill.context: Track the owners and unresolved commitments behind a customer escalation.

sections.title: Get a new customer to a first result

blocks.text: New customers did not buy a product tour. They bought whatever they need to get done this week. Strawberry builds the onboarding path from the signed scope, the sales handoff, the stakeholders, and the setup dependencies, pointed at the outcome the customer named.

During one pilot, a new RevOps user handed Strawberry a job that was half research and half operations: go through a set of competitor websites, work out which customers were featured on them, and explain how to log those companies in their own systems. A messy Tuesday-morning task, not a tutorial.
It came back as one output: the research, plus the next step written for that team's setup. The customer's reaction in the call notes was about as unambiguous as feedback gets.

items.context: Turn agreed goals and commitments into an owned path to first value.

sections.title: Turn resolved tickets into help docs

blocks.text: A good answer should not disappear when the ticket closes. Strawberry can turn a confirmed resolution into a help article the next customer can find, or show Product the pattern across several cases with the original tickets still linked.

A recruiting team sent one thread with four complaints: a licensing change they believed had happened, search failures getting worse, agents getting stuck, and credits going missing. The tempting move is to find one cause and explain everything with it.

Fritz, our support companion, treated them as four. The subscription was active and unchanged, so no licensing change. The missing credits were genuine use, almost the whole balance across hundreds of actions. The search problem got a targeted workaround. The stuck agents became a product signal for the team that owns it.
Then the part that makes the next ticket faster: the licensing answer became support documentation. The next person who asks gets it in a minute.

items.title: Publish the answer once
items.text: Turn a confirmed resolution or recurring question into help content the next customer can find, without duplicating an article that already exists.

skill.context: Turn verified current behavior into clear, findable customer documentation.

items.title: Show Product the pattern
items.text: Group feedback into themes, tensions, and examples with the original tickets still linked. A summary that informs the roadmap rather than pretending to be it.

skill.context: Turn customer feedback into themes, tensions, examples, and gaps with clear links to the sources.

blocks.text: Run one ticket from this week's queue through. It will get things wrong: too formal, escalated to the wrong team, citing a doc you retired months ago. Fix those and run another. After a handful, the corrections stop, and what is left is your team's support method, written down for the first time. Save it so the new hire handles a billing ticket the way your most experienced person does. Then put it on a schedule.

items.title: Set up the connected support system
items.text: Map the stack, learn from resolved cases, test the focused skills, and add Routines only after the manual flow works.

skill.context: Use Strawberry's published support method as a starting point, then adapt it to the systems and decisions your team already trusts.

items.title: Share the method with the team
items.text: Keep a trusted workflow as a team skill so colleagues follow the same checks, boundaries, and handoffs.

skill.context: Turn a trusted customer workflow into a shared team method with clear context, ownership, review points, and stop conditions.

blocks.text: A Routine repeats the check. It never grants permission to send, refund, change an account, file an issue, or publish. That stays with a person.
